As laid down in Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research v. Jaspal Singh, (2009) 7 SCC 330, the burden which ought to be discharged in civil proceedings in not as strict as in criminal cases and in order for any party to succeed, he/it is required to prove his/its case on the preponderance of probabilities.

The lack of a regulatory authorization or license does not automatically invalidate otherwise lawful commercial transactions unless the relevant law explicitly states that the contract is void as a consequence of the non-compliance.
The transaction itself must be for a lawful object and consideration, which is the case for the supply of raw vegetables.
41. In cases involving food supply, such as raw vegetables to canteens, the contract is for a legal commodity.
The requirement for a license (e.g., FSSAI or local municipal health license) primarily serves a regulatory and public policy purpose, ensuring hygiene and safety standards.

Operating without one is a regulatory offense, often punishable by fines or other penalties, but it does not inherently make the underlying commercial agreement for the sale of goods (the vegetables themselves) an "unlawful object" from the outset.
42. The defendant's case rests entirely on denial.
DW-1 categorically refused having received any goods or having had any business relationship with the plaintiff.
Yet, significantly, he produced no evidence to affirmatively prove his plea.
